## Three features in one file

Look at a classic raster VRT from GDAL and it's easy to see three
features sharing one XML file:

1. **Indirection.** The file holds references, not data. Reads go to
   other files, other locations, or several datasets presented as one.
2. **Metadata edits.** Attributes such as names, descriptions and labels
   are changed without touching the arrays.
3. **Operation chains.** Interpolation, regridding and the like are
   recorded as a lazy graph that runs when the data is read.

On this view, VRT bundles three jobs, and a modern stack would give each
one its own home: references in a virtual Zarr store, attributes in its
metadata, and the graph in a lazy engine.

As an inventory of what can appear in a VRT, that is fair. As an account
of why VRT works, and why newer tools keep arriving at parts of it but
never the whole, it misses most of the design. The three features describe
what goes *in* the file. The design is in what the file *is* and how it
*behaves*. Read that way, VRT is six properties, and they cut across the
three features:

| Property | In one line |
|---|---|
| **Closure** | the result is a dataset, so it opens anywhere and composes |
| **Names** | sources are dataset names, from any driver, through any I/O chain |
| **Placement** | windows of sources are pasted into windows of the output, aligned or not |
| **Assertion** | the VRT augments a source, supplying what it lacks and correcting what it gets wrong |
| **Deferral** | nothing is read until a window is requested |
| **Emission** | tools write it; almost no large VRT is written by hand |

## One format, three data models

VRT is GDAL's virtualization format, and it is first-class in all three of
GDAL's data models. The `VRT` driver serves classic and multidimensional
rasters, and `OGR_VRT` serves vector. A `vrt://` connection string is a
fourth form: a classic raster VRT with no file.

This post is mostly about **classic raster VRT**: a `<VRTDataset>` of
`<VRTRasterBand>` elements fed by sources (Simple, Complex, Averaged,
KernelFiltered), plus derived bands and warped VRTs. The full grammar is in
[`gdalvrt.xsd`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OSGeo/gdal/master/frmts/vrt/data/gdalvrt.xsd).
The other forms of virtualization in GDAL show where classic raster VRT
ends:

- **`vrt://` strings**: one source dataset with `gdal_translate` options
  written as a URI, so there is no file.
- **Multidimensional VRT**: groups, dimensions and arrays. Sources are
  placed by index slabs, and derived arrays add View, Transpose, Resample
  and Grid steps.
- **Vector VRT** (`OGRVRTDataSource`): layers built from other layers,
  with fields, geometry from columns, SQL, regions and unions.
- **GTI** (sources as rows of a vector layer) and **GDALG** (a saved
  `gdal` pipeline that opens as a dataset): close relatives, not VRT.

All six properties are present in classic raster VRT, and the sections
below describe them there. The other forms come in where they show a
property more strongly or less, and the table near the end compares all
four.

## Closure

A VRT is a dataset. It opens wherever GDAL opens a dataset, every GDAL
tool reads it, and it can be the source of another VRT. That is not a
packaging detail; it is why VRT composes. A SQL view has the same idea.

A source can be another VRT in two ways. It can be a `.vrt` file, by path
or through any `/vsi` chain, and that nesting goes as deep as you like. Or
it can be a `vrt://` string. GDAL splits the string at the first `?`,
opens what comes before it, and always runs `GDALTranslate` onto a new VRT
dataset, applying the options after the `?` if there are any. So
`vrt://f.tif` is the source wrapped in a transient identity VRT, and a
`vrt://` string does not nest: everything after the first `?` belongs to
the outermost string. And because the options are `gdal_translate`'s, a
`vrt://` string cannot warp. The other forms are closed in their own
models (a multidimensional VRT can read another, and a vector VRT layer
can come from another vector VRT), and GDALG extends closure to whole
pipelines.

## Names

A source is a dataset name, not a file path. It can be any driver
(`NETCDF:"f.nc":sst`), any `/vsi` chain
(`/vsizip/{/vsicurl/https://host/a.zip}/b.tif`), any subdataset, or another
VRT. Anything GDAL can open can be placed. A name can even cross data
models: `vrt://f.zarr?transpose=/sst:1,2` picks two dimensions of a
multidimensional array to form a classic raster, with the rest as bands,
and that string can sit in `SourceFilename` like any other. That reach is
where the "indirection" of the three-feature view really lives. VRT
redirects to *datasets*, not to bytes.

The `/vsi` chains are GDAL's virtual file system, one of its quiet modules.
Python reaches it directly as `gdal.VSIFile`, a file-like object over any
`/vsi` path. rasterio adopts it under its own abstractions (`s3://` URLs,
`MemoryFile`).

The same names are used in every form; vector VRT adds open options beside
the name. No schema types the name: in `gdalvrt.xsd`, `SourceFilename` is a
plain `xs:string`, with a `relativeToVRT` attribute. What a name means is
defined by the drivers' open code, which is why names are the hardest part
to carry outside GDAL.

## Placement

A window of a source is pasted into a window of the output. Offsets can be
fractional, sizes can differ, and sources can overlap. When a request
arrives, GDAL works out which source window feeds which output window and
resamples where the sizes or offsets require it. This is the second half
of "indirection" (several datasets as one), and GDAL excels at quietly
providing this capability.

In classic raster VRT, `SrcRect` and `DstRect` are arbitrary 2D windows,
and every `ComplexSource` can carry its own resampling. Multidimensional
VRT is stricter: it places sources by integer slabs (`SourceSlab`,
`DestSlab`), and resampling is a separate derived step.

Non-aligned placement works because GDAL's `RasterIO` has no alignment
requirement. A VRT source turns the requested output window into a
floating-point source window and passes it on with the source's
resampling method. With nearest neighbour the fractional offsets are
rounded to the nearest pixel; with bilinear, cubic and the rest, `RasterIO`
interpolates across the fractional window. A classic VRT never reprojects
a source: placement assumes one CRS. Reprojection is the warper's job,
either as a warped VRT over a whole dataset or, in GTI, per source
whenever a source's CRS differs from the index's.

GTI exists because classic VRT stops scaling here. Every source is listed
in the XML, so opening a VRT parses every source entry, and nothing
indexes them in space. GTI keeps placement and moves the sources into rows
of an indexed vector layer.

Placement is also where the three-feature split breaks down. In real
mosaics, indirection *is* an operation:

- **USGS 3DEP 1 arc-second seamless VRT** (3,817 tiles, read 2026-11-05):
  every tile is placed at a fractional offset and read with bilinear
  resampling. The VRT writes its pixel size as 2.777778e-4 degree, while
  the tiles sit on a 1/3600-degree pitch, so the tile offsets drift by up
  to 0.10 px across the mosaic. The "redirection" becomes an interpolation
  on every read, caused by one rounded constant. The tiles also overlap
  their neighbours by 6 pixels.
- **Copernicus DEM GLO-30 as one VRT** (26,475 tiles): 55 % of the tiles
  are resampled to the common grid, because their native widths change
  with latitude. Every one of the remaining 45 % overlaps a neighbour by a
  pixel.

A virtual Zarr store (kerchunk, VirtualiZarr, Icechunk) can hold none of
these placements. It references chunks that line up exactly with its own
grid. By contrast, the GHRSST MUR daily COGs as a multidimensional VRT
(38,365 placements across five arrays) are all aligned, identity
placements. For data shaped like that, the VRT and a byte-reference
store carry the same information, and the three-feature split works.

## Assertion

The VRT augments a source, supplying what it lacks and correcting what it
gets wrong, without copying a byte. The assertions that matter change what
the bytes *mean*: a CRS for a file that has none, a corrected
geotransform, a nodata value, a scale and offset. Seven of the
[keys listed in the docs](https://gdal.org/en/stable/drivers/raster/vrt.html#vrt-connection-string)
for the `vrt://` syntax begin with `a_` for "assign" (`a_srs`, `a_ullr`,
`a_gt`, `a_nodata`, `a_scale`, `a_offset`, `a_coord_epoch`). Metadata
repair is one of the main reasons people write VRTs at all.

In classic raster VRT the assertions are `SRS`, `GeoTransform`,
`NoDataValue`, `Offset`, `Scale`, `ColorInterp`, band `Description` and
metadata. Renaming barely applies, because classic bands are numbered and
a description is all they have. It matters in the other forms: arrays and
dimensions are named in multidimensional VRT, and fields are renamed and
retyped in vector VRT. Multidimensional VRT can also assert whole
coordinates (`RegularlySpacedValues`) and dimension types, and vector VRT
asserts geometry type, layer CRS and geometry built from columns.

The 3DEP case shows why assertion belongs next to placement. An exact
pixel size of 1/3600 degree would make every one of its placements
integer, and remove the resampling entirely.

## Deferral

Opening a VRT plans; it does not read. Ask for a window, and GDAL works
out which sources, which source windows and which operations that window
needs before it touches a byte, with the block cache underneath. So a VRT
is cheap to make, cheap to pass on, and cheap to throw away.

Every form works this way. The plan, though, lives only inside GDAL's
objects. No form exposes it as data that another process, language or
engine could take.

## Emission

Tools compile *to* VRT. That is how VRTs with thousands of sources exist,
and why most VRTs in the wild are tool output rather than written by hand.
Classic raster VRT is written by `gdalbuildvrt`, `gdal_translate -of VRT`,
`gdalwarp -of VRT`, and `gdal raster mosaic` and `stack`.
Multidimensional VRT is written by `gdal mdim mosaic` (GDAL 3.12) and
`gdal mdim convert`. Vector VRTs are mostly written by hand or by
scripts, `vrt://` strings by people and by packages that build dataset
names, and GDALG by `gdal` pipelines.

The output need not be a file. VRT is XML text, and the text is itself a
dataset name: `gdal.Open()` accepts a string that begins `<VRTDataset`.
Then `gdal_translate -of VRT in.tif /vsistdout/` writes it to a pipe, and
`gdal.Translate('', src, format='VRT')` builds one in memory, with the XML
available from `GetMetadata('xml:VRT')`. So a pipeline that emits VRT is
not bound to files. The recipe travels as a string and opens wherever it
lands, as long as its source names resolve there.

## Operations come from placement and assertion

The third feature of the three-feature view is real, but it is not a
property of its own. It is what placement and assertion become once they
compute values.

In classic raster VRT these are derived bands with pixel functions, warped
VRTs, and the per-source operations of `ComplexSource` (scale, offset,
LUT, nodata), `KernelFilteredSource` and `AveragedSource`. The most common
operation in practice is the one hidden inside placement: a resample
whenever a source window and output window differ. The other forms have
derived arrays in multidimensional VRT, SQL and reprojected layers in
vector VRT, and whole pipelines in GDALG.

## Six properties, four forms

| | Classic raster | `vrt://` | Multidimensional | Vector |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Closure | full, nests | doesn't nest | full | full |
| Names | full | the string is a name | full | full, plus open options |
| Placement | arbitrary 2D windows, resampled per source | one window | integer slabs; resampling is a derived step | none; regions and unions |
| Assertion | CRS, geotransform, nodata, scale, offset | the seven `a_` keys | plus coordinates, dimension types, names | geometry, CRS, field names and types |
| Deferral | full | full | full | full |
| Emission | many GDAL tools | people and packages | `gdal mdim mosaic`, `gdal mdim convert` | mostly by hand |
| Operations | pixel functions, warped VRT, per-source ops | translate options | derived array steps | SQL, reprojection |

Classic raster VRT is the strongest form of placement and emission. It is
the reason "VRT" means a mosaic or a stack, most of the time, and it is
the family the three-feature view was drawn from. It is also where that
view goes wrong: each feature can be pointed to in the XML, but in
placement, indirection and computation are one thing.

## Each property turns up elsewhere

| Turns up as | Where |
|---|---|
| byte-level references, plus history | kerchunk, VirtualiZarr, Icechunk |
| sources as rows with statistics, so planning becomes pruning | Iceberg, Delta, Lance; GDAL's own GTI |
| the plan as a value an engine optimises | Polars, DuckDB, DataFusion, JAX |
| assertion as declared metadata | Zarr v3 attributes and conventions |
| saved operation chains that reopen | `gdal` pipelines and `.gdalg.json` |
| memory shared across languages and processes | Arrow, mizu |

Each of these does its part better than VRT does. None does all six, and
outside GDAL none composes misaligned windows of arbitrary formats by
name. Inside GDAL that is classic raster VRT, and GTI as its answer to
scale.

## What software ingesting VRT needs to model

Splitting VRT into parts is the right instinct for an ecosystem that wants
each part done well in its own place. Software that ingests a VRT, reading
the XML itself rather than handing it to GDAL, needs to model two things.

1. **Placement as an operation.** Byte references are exact only for
   aligned data. For model output stored one file per step, a VRT lowers
   to byte references with nothing lost. For imagery mosaics, placement
   *is* an operation, so indirection and regridding have to be modelled
   together. A converter from VRT to virtual Zarr should say, source by
   source, which placements become byte references exactly and why the
   rest cannot.
2. **Closure, names and deferral.** A source can be another VRT, a
   source name means whatever GDAL's drivers say it means, and nothing is
   read until a window is asked for. Software that models only the
   top-level XML reads one VRT file, not the format.

*The counts above come from reading each VRT's XML, with no source opened:
the [3DEP 1 arc-second VRT](https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/Elevation/1/TIFF/USGS_Seamless_DEM_1.vrt)
on 2026-11-05, the
[GHRSST MUR VRT](https://data.source.coop/ausantarctic/ghrsst-mur-v2/ghrsst-mur-v2.vrt)
on 2026-11-06, and the
[COP30 VRT](https://opentopography.s3.sdsc.edu/raster/COP30/COP30_hh.vrt)
on 2026-10-19.*
